claims.claim: Jenny Turner's 2001 LRB essay dismisses Tolkien's prose style in passing without analysis.
claims.source: Jenny Turner 2001, as reported in Curry, 'The Critical Response to Tolkien's Fiction'

claims.claim: The reader's impression of archaicity comes partly from over-use of nineteenth-century fiction words, avoidance of modern-world words, and dense coinages, unusual grammar and rare or obsolescent words.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation into The Lord of the Rings' (CL2017)

claims.claim: Keywords shared with nineteenth-century novels cluster in landscape, position/direction (whither, thither, thence, yonder, afar), warfare, and descriptive verbs/adjectives, many obsolete when Tolkien wrote.
claims.quote: so many of the keywords used to describe its settings

claims.claim: Tolkien borrows words such as valour, valiant and corslet from his Beowulf translation and stretches them beyond their Old and Middle English range.
claims.quote: Tolkien borrows a host of words from his translation of Beowulf

claims.feature: modern words in old grammatical patterns
claims.claim: Even core modern words are used in nineteenth-century patterns, e.g. 'a black smoke' with the indefinite article, rare in modern fiction.
claims.quote: tends to use many of these words in nineteenth-century patterns

claims.claim: Tolkien follows a modernist tendency in his abundant manner-laden verbs: clutch, cower, flicker, gleam, glimmer, loom, peer, plod, stride, twist.
Words key only to Tolkien (dingle, fen, glades, starless, lore-masters, wolf-riders, yesteryear, yuledays, along/among/outwards) are rare but not archaic and together create otherworldliness.
claims.quote: an atmosphere of medievalism or otherworldliness

claims.claim: Tolkien prefers the most homely collocations available yet uses everyday adjectives like 'great' in unusual pairings, and his key semantic domains (speed, size, loudness) point to hyperbole.
claims.quote: a marked preference for the most homely collocations available

claims.claim: Far from amateurish, the prose deploys several centuries of linguistic development, putting old words to new uses and vice versa.
Keyword, n-gram and collocation methods show the style of The Lord of the Rings relies heavily on nineteenth-century novels and on Tolkien's Beowulf translation.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a Stylist: Key Words and Key Collocations' (2021), ch. 2
claims.quote: relies heavily on the nineteenth-century novel

claims.claim: The full subtlety of Tolkien's collocations has escaped both casual readers and literary critics.
claims.quote: escaped both the casual reader's and the literary critic's notice

claims.claim: The third-person narrator presents the point of view of a group of characters, usually hobbits, recorded in ordinary language.
Other passages carry an archaic diction reminiscent of ancient epic and Macpherson's Ossian, conveying an omniscient point of view tied to epic characters like Aragorn.
claims.quote: archaic diction, reminiscent of ancient epic poetry

claims.claim: Limiting point of view to certain characters' perceptions, thoughts and feelings follows nineteenth-century novelistic practice.
Thomas calls the narrator of The Lord of the Rings self-effacing, unintrusive and vanishing, and counts ten different viewpoints in the opening chapter.
claims.source: Paul Edmund Thomas, 'Some of Tolkien's Narrators' (2000), as quoted in Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, ch. 4
